structure.overview: Mr. Wu appealed the Final Second Review Decision by the Canada Revenue Agency denying his eligibility for the Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB) due to insufficient income proof. The Attorney General of Canada defended the decision as reasonable and procedurally fair, challenging the admissibility of new evidence. The Federal Court found the decision reasonable and procedurally fair, rejected Mr. Wu's procedural fairness and Charter claims, and refused to admit new evidence, dismissing the appeal.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu argues the Final Second Reviewer breached procedural fairness and made an unreasonable decision ignoring his income proof and alleges coercion violating Charter s 7 rights.
idea_list: Charter s 7 rights breach by coercion

citations.cite: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s 7, Part I of the Constitution Act, 1982, being Schedule B to the Canada Act 1982 (UK), 1982, c 11
citations.why: Mr. Wu alleges breach of his Charter s 7 rights

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent, Attorney General of Canada, preliminarily challenges admissibility of some evidence and defends the Final Second Review Decision as reasonable and procedurally fair.
idea_list: defence of decision's reasonableness and fairness

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court finds the Final Second Review Decision procedurally fair and reasonable, refusing to allow Mr. Wu more evidence after multiple CRA opportunities.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: The CRB Act provisions define the Minister, impose burden of proof on applicant, and allow Minister to reconsider eligibility within 36 months after payment.

citations.why: statutory provisions relevant to the case

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu submitted various documents to CRA in August 2022, including letters, tax assessments, and receipts totaling $5,750.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The First Reviewer found Mr. Wu ineligible for CRB due to insufficient income proof and inability to contact him for more information.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: CRA notified Mr. Wu of the First Decision denying CRB eligibility for not meeting the $5,000 income threshold.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Initial Second Reviewer found Mr. Wu ineligible again due to insufficient income proof and inability to contact him after two attempts.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: CRA notified Mr. Wu of the Initial Second Review Decision denying CRB eligibility for not meeting income requirements.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The new officer spoke with Mr. Wu in January 2024, who explained his employment and babysitting income paid in cash without documentation.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu submitted various documents in February 2024, including medical records, handwritten income calculations, and tax returns.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: In March 2024, Mr. Wu explained his cancer diagnosis, employment history, and lack of documentation supporting his income claims.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: In May 2024, the officer explained babysitting income was casual, not business, and Mr. Wu claimed additional caregiving work paid by cheque.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu uploaded documents in May 2024 including letters, employment confirmation, cheques, and job applications.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: In June 2024, another CRA officer was assigned to review Mr. Wu’s CRB eligibility.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: In June 2024, the new officer spoke with Mr. Wu who described his employment, babysitting, caregiving, and was given a deadline for more documents.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu uploaded documents in June 2024 including letters, text messages, T4A slip, and cheques from caregiving work.

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: In July 2024, a Final Second Reviewer was assigned to continue reviewing Mr. Wu’s CRB eligibility.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Final Second Reviewer spoke with Mr. Wu in July 2024 and confirmed previously stated information.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Final Second Reviewer explained the review process and income calculation periods to Mr. Wu in July 2024.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Final Second Reviewer’s notes list Mr. Wu’s submitted documents and income amounts for 2019, 2020, and 2021 showing insufficient income.

citations.cite: Aryan v Canada (Attorney General), 2022 FC 139 at para 22
citations.why: cited as part of the Final Second Reviewer’s reasons

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Final Second Reviewer analyzed Mr. Wu’s documents and found total income below $5,000 for relevant periods, denying CRB eligibility.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The party challenging the decision must prove serious shortcomings making it unjustified, unintelligible, or lacking transparency to overturn it.

citations.why: sets burden and test for unreasonableness

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Procedural fairness breaches are reviewed on correctness; fairness is context-specific and assessed by factors from Baker and Vavilov.

citations.cite: Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54
citations.why: correctness standard for procedural fairness breaches

citations.cite: Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 1999 CanLII 699 (SCC), [1999] 2 SCR 817 at paras 22-23

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The AGC identifies several exhibits in Mr. Wu’s affidavit that were not before the Final Second Reviewer.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court agrees with the AGC’s position on the inadmissibility of the new evidence not before the Final Second Reviewer.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court explains the general rule against new evidence on judicial review and lists exceptions from Access Copyright.

citations.why: general rule on new evidence admissibility

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court finds Mr. Wu’s new evidence does not meet exceptions and would improperly supplement the record, thus inadmissible.

citations.cite: Federal Courts Act, RSC 1985, c F-7, s 18.1(4)(d)
citations.why: court’s role limited to reviewing existing record

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Court will not consider new evidence and will review the Final Second Review Decision only for reasonableness and procedural fairness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu has not shown serious shortcomings; superficial flaws are insufficient to overturn the decision.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu argues CERB eligibility should apply to CRB, but the AGC and court reject this, citing Joodaki confirming separate eligibility.

citations.cite: Joodaki v Canada (Attorney General), 2024 FC 260 at para 17
citations.why: Confirms CRB and CERB have separate eligibility requirements

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu submits his CRB application date means earnings from Oct 15, 2019 to Oct 9, 2020 should be counted to meet $5,000 threshold.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu contends the Final Second Reviewer's decision lacks justification for ignoring his tax returns and records proving income eligibility.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The May 22, 2024 letter about $2,200 income was not before the Final Second Reviewer, so its omission is not faulted.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu submitted cheques from A. Lau and others on May 24, 2024, some dated before October 2019, which do not count for the income period.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Additional cheques from Mr. Lau to Mr. Wu were submitted on June 28, 2024, dated early 2020.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: AGC admits Final Second Reviewer omitted Mr. Lau payments but argues Mr. Wu admitted these were gifts for non-profit services in a June 14, 2024 call.
idea_list: AGC cites Mr. Wu's admission of gifts in call

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court finds it reasonable for Final Second Reviewer to exclude Mr. Lau payments as non-eligible gifts from non-profit services.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu argues calculation period error, but even including all amounts, he does not meet the $5,000 income threshold.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu claims CRA breached procedural fairness by ignoring his income documents and denying him a fair chance to respond.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu relies on Cameron to argue procedural fairness breach due to CRA's failure to accommodate disability and broken promises.
idea_list: Summary of Cameron's procedural fairness findings

citations.why: Mr. Wu cites Cameron for procedural fairness breach
Cameron cites Canadian Pacific on procedural fairness

citations.cite: Agraira v Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 SCC 36 at para 96
citations.why: Cameron cites Agraira on legitimate expectations doctrine

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court rejects Mr. Wu's procedural fairness claim, noting he was not disabled, had no promised procedure, and submitted documents multiple times.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Procedural fairness requires the party to know the case and respond; deference does not override this fundamental right, citing Canadian Pacific.

citations.why: Emphasizes procedural fairness and right to be heard despite deference

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu alleges coercion by CRA Officer violating his section 7 Charter rights, but provides no evidence or legal support.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court finds no evidence of coercion and dismisses Mr. Wu's section 7 Charter claim for lack of basis and procedural steps, citing Ibrahim.

citations.cite: Ibrahim v Canada (Attorney General), 2023 FC 1357 at para 14
citations.why: Mr. Wu failed to meet requirements to pursue Charter claim

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Wu's section 7 Charter claim is not considered by the Court.
